sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into SQL queries over increasingly complex databases. However, widely used benchmarks evaluate questions independently, overlooking settings where earlier queries over the same database can supply joins or calculations for a new question. We introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) to measure the accuracy and cost of adapting historical SQL. HARE comprises 1,600 requests derived from a fixed pool of 823 verified queries across four datasets. Annotations record which components each request preserves and which edits it requires, distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial reuse. Our method, MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and mappings from domain concepts to schema elements. MEM-SQL uses a layer only if every requirement assigned to it has a match above that layer's threshold. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), MEM-SQL consults the schema only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges retrieved evidence insufficient. Across six language models on HARE, mean execution accuracy rises from 37.1% for Direct Generation without history to 50.0% for MEM-SQL, with 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency on average. Further analysis shows that requests reusing several verified queries remain a bottleneck, with accuracy falling from 56.7% to 29.7%, most sharply when reused components must be placed in a new query structure or combined with a shared join. Applying OSL to three other memory designs consistently reduces generation cost, while its accuracy benefit depends on the memory design. Verified history can thus make generation both more accurate and cheaper, but its value depends on the evidence retained and when the system consults the schema.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Text-to-SQL translates natural language question into SQL query that retrieves the answer (Hong et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Its benchmarks have grown in scope and difficulty. Spider tests generalization across databases (Yu et al., 2018), BIRD asks questions that depend on database values (Li et al., 2023), and Spider 2.0 introduces enterprise tasks over schemas that can exceed 1,000 columns (Lei et al., 2024). Recent systems retrieve relevant schema elements, generate candidate queries, and test them against database (Talaei et al., 2024; Pourreza et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026; Pei et al., 2025). AskData achieves 83.40% execution accuracy on BIRD test set by pairing offline meta-data extraction with iterative, draft SQL driven schema linking to resolve schema ambiguities (Shkapenyuk et al., 2025; BIRD Team, 2026). However, benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023) evaluate questions independently, overlooking setting in which users repeatedly query the same database (Ma et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). Verified queries from an earlier request may already answer new question or supply part of the computation it requires. Access to these queries can spare the system of reconstructing the same logic from schema (Regmi & Pun, 2024), costly step on large databases (Lian et al., 2024; Wang et al., *Equal Contribution Project Lead

sections.content: 2025a). Yet query can still execute even when some of its logic no longer matches the new request (Zhong et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2025a; Pei et al., 2026). To assess the value of query history, benchmark must identify what carries over between requests and measure how access to that history affects accuracy and generation cost (Peng et al., 2025; Piao et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2026), across different types of edits. To bridge this gap, we introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark). total of 1,600 requests are derived from 823 verified queries drawn from Spider (Yu et al., 2018), BIRD (Li et al., 2023), Spider 2.0 (Lei et al., 2024), and BEAVER (Chen et al., 2024). Six primitive and six composite categories specify which historical components new request retains and which edits it permits. For example, request may preserve join path but change the calculation over the joined rows. These annotations make it possible to distinguish adapting complete query from assembling partial evidence. Validation checks both the answer and the intended relationship to history, so an executable query alone does not qualify. Effective adaptation also depends on what system chooses to remember (Zhou et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025c). Agent memory systems organize past interactions to support long-term question answering (Xu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026a; Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). In Text-to-SQL, prior work reuses successful queries, corrections, and execution traces (Yang et al., 2026b; Biswal et al., 2026). This raises the question of which parts reliable Text-to-SQL system should retain from verified query, and how it should decide if retrieved evidence suffices for new question. To address this question, we present MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL). Inspired by hierarchical agent memories (Wang et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2024), its three memory layers expose complete query templates, reusable SELECT blocks, and schema concepts. This lets new requests draw on the desired level of historical computations. Searchable descriptions connect new wording to stored SQL structures and column mappings (Koukouvinis et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Retrieval checks coverage separately for each requirement, and layer contributes only if every assigned requirement has match above required threshold. strong match therefore cannot hide an uncovered requirement. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), the system consults schema only when no layer qualifies or generator judges selected evidence insufficient, rather than relying solely on model uncertainty (Deng et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). Experiments across six language models show that accuracy and efficiency can improve together. MEM-SQL raises mean execution accuracy from 37.1% for Direct Generation to 50.0%, while reducing input tokens and latency. The ablations reveal distinct roles for the memory layers: templates contribute most to accuracy, while query blocks matter especially for composition. Further analysis shows that the gains concentrate on requests that keep historical structure, while composing evidence from several verified queries remains difficult for every method. Applying OSL to three other memory designs (Gao et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2026b) lowers both costs in every comparison, but its accuracy benefit varies with the ability of designs to retrieve complete evidence. This separates broadly transferable efficiency gain from the harder problem of deciding whether retrieved evidence is sufficient. Our contributions are as follows. (i) We introduce HARE to measure the accuracy and cost of reusing verified SQL queries. Source annotations distinguish whole-query adaptation from the reuse of individual components. (ii) We develop MEM-SQL to retrieve evidence and check coverage at three granularities, supporting both complete-query adaptation and composition from historical components. (iii) We conduct analysis on OSL transferability to three other memory designs and found that with good memory design, deferring schema consultation improves accuracy and reduces input tokens, latency.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Text-to-SQL Benchmarks. Early benchmarks progressed from single-table querying in WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017) to complex cross-domain parsing in Spider (Yu et al., 2018), with SParC (Yu et al., 2019b) and CoSQL (Yu et al., 2019a) extending evaluation to multi-turn context and dialogue. In the LLM era, BIRD (Li et al., 2023) emphasized database values, external knowledge, and SQL efficiency. BEAVER (Chen et al., 2024) and Spider 2.0 (Lei et al., 2024) subsequently introduced enterprise workloads involving

HARE provides explicit labels for historical query reuse. It enables controlled evaluation of adaptation accuracy and efficiency. Text-to-SQL Methods. Neural Text-to-SQL evolved from sequence-to-sequence generation (Zhong et al., 2017) to schema-aware (Wang et al., 2020) and constrained pretrained parsers (Scholak et al., 2021). LLMera work includes DIN-SQLs decomposed prompting (Pourreza & Rafiei, 2023), CHESSs agentic retrieval and validation (Talaei et al., 2024), CHASE-SQLs candidate generation and selection (Pourreza et al., 2024). Later work developed pseudo-schema grounding in Gen-SQL (Shi et al., 2025), tree search in Alpha-SQL (Li et al., 2025a), synthetic-data training in OmniSQL (Li et al., 2025b), autonomous schema exploration in AutoLink (Wang et al., 2025b), and execution-aware reinforcement learning in ReEx-SQL (Dai et al., 2026). MEM-SQL reuses verified query history to answer new Text-to-SQL requests, enabling accurate SQL generation with reduced token and latency overhead. Memory for Text-to-SQL. Text-to-SQL memory spans demonstrations, domain knowledge, and execution experience. DAIL-SQL (Gao et al., 2023) retrieves demonstrations, while LPE-SQL (Chu et al., 2024) and Memo-SQL (Yang et al., 2026b) retain successful queries and corrective experience. Cook et al. (2025) distill interaction feedback into question, subtask, and database-fact memories for continual learning. AgentSM (Biswal et al., 2026) reuses exploration trajectories, and Wang et al. (2026b) learn retrieval over episodeand turn-level memories for interactive Text-to-SQL agents. SDAM (Xu et al., 2026) binds reflected rules to schemas, whereas BIRD-History (Zhou et al., 2026b) retrieves SQL queries and components. Tk-Boost (Agarwal et al., 2026) supplies applicability-conditioned corrective knowledge. MIRA (Liu et al., 2026c) verifies memory for post-generation repair. MaP-SQL (Jeong et al., 2026) uses memory for candidate selection. MEM-SQL introduces layered SQL memory architecture with coverage-gated routing. This enables accurate and efficient reuse of historical SQL knowledge.

sections.title: 3 HARE
sections.content: Text-to-SQL requests often vary date range, target entity, metric, or grouping while reusing earlier query structures, intermediate computations, or schema knowledge. Evaluating each request in isolation obscures whether system can exploit this historical overlap. HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) measures how effectively and efficiently Text-to-SQL systems reuse verified history. Each HARE request is derived from verified historical queries and records both retained components and modifications made.

sections.title: 3.1 Sources and Categories
sections.content: We draw verified historical questionSQL pairs from cross-domain benchmarks Spider (Yu et al., 2018), BIRD (Li et al., 2023), and enterprise benchmarks Spider 2.0 (Lei et al., 2024), BEAVER (Chen et al., 2024). We construct new requests in six categories according to retained evidence and permited changes. (1) Rephrase rewords question without changing its SQL. (2) Parametric Changes change literal values while preserving full query structure. (3) Component Parametric Changes change values in reused intermediate computation while allowing different surrounding logic. (4) Structural Changes retain an intermediate computation and incorporate it into new query structure. (5) Shared Joins preserve historical join path while changing filters, grouping, or other clauses. (6) Shared Concepts reuse column mappings, metric definitions, or relationships to express new query logic. These categories span whole-query, component, and schema-level reuse. We also define six composite categories that combine pairs of these reuse types.

sections.title: 3.3 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Source Selection. We select lead query whose SQL contains the evidence request must retain. For shared join, for example, the join predicate must occur inside the intermediate computation to be reused. Among eligible queries, we favor those selected least often before breaking ties in favor of queries whose tables have been sampled less often to achieve balanced coverage of underlying tables and query structures. Companion Selection. All sources for request come from the same database. Single-category requests use the lead alone except for structural changes and shared joins that allow up to two companions sharing table with the lead. composite request can draw up to six queries. The category specifies what the new SQL must retain. In Figure 2, two of three available sources supply the evidence for composite query. Constrained Generation. For each category, we specify evidence that must be preserved and permitted edits called business rules. Business rules constrain changes to dates, thresholds, ranking, measures, grouping, and join paths. For example, parametric change edits must preserve the SQL structure while structural changes must retain selected intermediate computation. For composite requests, edit rules apply separately to evidence retained for each reuse type. Using each source group and schema, sampled values, join paths, domain knowledge and category rules, GLM5.3-Flash (GLM-5 Team, 2026) generates three candidates. Candidate Validation. We parse and deduplicate candidates, then check execution validity, semantic alignment, and reuse preservation. Execution must succeed and return at least one non-NULL row. Claude Opus 5.5 reviews question SQL agreement, consistency with domain knowledge, and category constraints, and repairs failed candidates. Failed candidates receive up to three repair attempts that may revise the question and SQL while keeping the historical sources and target category fixed. Only candidates passing all checks enter HARE. Appendix gives the full details for each reuse category.

sections.content: Figure 3 shows how MEM-SQL builds memory from verified queries and uses it to answer new question. Offline, MEM-SQL stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and schema concepts that map domain terms to columns and relationships. Each item pairs searchable description with the SQL structure or schema mapping it describes. new question can therefore reuse historical join even when it calls for different calculation. At inference, MEM-SQL identifies what evidence the question needs from each layer and retrieves candidates for each requirement. layer contributes evidence only if every requirement assigned to it has match above that layers threshold. The generator combines evidence from the qualifying layers. With OSL, the system performs schema linking only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges the combined evidence insufficient. sections.title: 4.2.1 Memory Representation
sections.content: MEM-SQL organizes each databases memory into three layers comprising whole-query templates MT , reusable query components MC, and schema concepts MS: = MT MC MS. (1) memory item couples natural language description di with structured payload pi and dense description embedding ei: mi = (di, pi, ei), where ei = E(di). (2) The text encoder enables dense semantic retrieval, while the payload pi preserves the exact SQL syntax, subquery structure, or schema mapping required for generation. Metadata on historical source accompany each item.

sections.content: Templates MT . Each historical query becomes complete skeleton in which literal values, sort directions, LIMIT/OFFSET clauses, aggregates, conditional expressions, window functions, and grouping keys are replaced by typed placeholders called slots. For example, question about Lewis Hamiltons average lap time in the 2009 Malaysian Grand Prix yields SELECT agg FROM races JOIN lapTimes ... WHERE year = year AND name = name. Components MC. component is SELECT block from an outer query, WITH clause, subquery, or set It keeps its FROM, JOIN, and clause structure operation branch that contains joins or supported clauses. in one item, masks projections and literals as in templates, and records candidate key relationships for its join predicates. Nested blocks become separate components. The same query about Lewis Hamilton yields the join and clause preserving component FROM races JOIN lapTimes ON join1 JOIN drivers ON join2 WHERE ..., where join1 records lapTimes.raceId = races.raceId. Schema Concepts MS. An LLM extracts semantic roles, their column mappings, and join relationships from historical questions, SQL, and schemas, dropping request specific ranking and output constraints. For example, the concept lap time maps to lapTimes.milliseconds and joins lapTimes.driverId = drivers.driverId and lapTimes.raceId = races.raceId. For each candidate, MEM-SQL retrieves the item with the closest description in the same database and layer. The two merge only if their descriptions have cosine similarity of at least 0.9 and their stored SQL or schema mappings are equivalent. Otherwise, an LLM checks whether nearby items jointly cover the candidate and MEM-SQL inserts it if coverage is incomplete. Each historical query links to the items created from it, the targets of any merges, and any items that already cover its information. This preserves the link to the source even when no new item enters the store. Appendix B.1 gives the layer-specific merge criteria.

sections.title: 4.2.3 On-demand Schema Linking (OSL)
sections.content: With OSL, the generator receives the question q, its rewrite q, the requirements r, domain knowledge K, and the selected evidence B. If every layer fails the gate and is empty, the schema-linking route runs immediately. Otherwise, the synthesizer first attempts generation from alone. If the model declares the evidence insufficient, schema linking L(q, D) supplies the missing context before synthesis with (B, L(q, D)). Raw schema details are thus fetched only when historical evidence leaves gaps. MEM-SQL checks the generated query with database dry run and attempts to repair it if validation fails. Appendix provides detailed prompt templates.

sections.title: 5.1 Setup
sections.content: Backbones. We evaluate every method on two closed-weight backbones, Gemini4-Argon (Google DeepMind, 2026) and GPT6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026). We also test four open-weight models, GLM5.3-Flash (GLM-5 Team, 2026), Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), and Granite4.2-8B (IBM Granite Team, 2026). Baselines. We evaluate four baselines. Direct Generation provides reference without query history. DAIL-SQL (Gao et al., 2023) represents demonstration selection for few-shot Text-to-SQL. We adapt AMEM (Xu et al., 2025b) to test general-purpose agent memory on questionSQL pairs. BIRD-History (Zhou et al., 2026b) provides task-specific retriever for historical SQL logs. Appendix B.3 describes the adaptations for the three memory baselines. Metrics. We adopt execution accuracy (EX) to measure accuracy, and input tokens and latency to measure efficiency. We measure EX as percentage of 1,600 HARE requests whose generated SQL returns gold execution result. Appendix B.4 specifies how execution results are compared. We report mean input tokens (k) and end-to-end pipeline latency (s) per request, including recorded cost of reused decomposition and schema-linking steps. We compare latency only within each backbone because serving conditions vary.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Table 1 shows that verified history can improve accuracy while reducing generation cost. Relative to Direct Generation, MEM-SQL raises EX by 12.9 points and reduces input tokens by 76.6% and latency by 68.8% on average. It leads the three memory baselines on every backbone. These baselines use the Unconditional Schema Linking (USL) policy, consulting the schema for every request. MEM-SQL completes 95.4% of requests from memory on average, which helps explain the cost reduction: most requests avoid schema linking. The simultaneous accuracy gain is consistent with verified computation providing useful guidance. Section 5.5 examines the remaining aggregation and grouping errors, while Section 6 tests OSL separately.

sections.title: 5.3.1 Retrieval Design Ablation
sections.content: We carried out ablation studies on MEM-SQLs retrieval design using separate calibration set of 240 questions from HARE covering all twelve categories to quantify impacts of removing each retrieval component. We calculate recall rate, defined as the percentage of questions which retrieved at least one item from every historical source the question reuses in all required layers. We also report recall rate per layer, defined as percentage of questions retrieving at least one item from every corresponding source in that layer. As shown from Table 3, requirement-specific retrieval improves coverage while keeping the evidence bundle compact. Retrieval atoms raise micro recall from 56.67% to 94.58% over using the full question within each layer. Flat retrieval has slightly higher recall, but layered atoms return 37.7% fewer items per question. On the evaluation requests, retrieval atoms improve EX over full-question retrieval on all six backbones, by 1.8 points on average. Flat retrieval matches or slightly exceeds MEM-SQL on five backbones, but uses more input tokens on all six. Layered selection therefore controls prompt size while retaining competitive accuracy.

sections.title: 5.4.1 Performance by Category
sections.content: 1 Accuracy Analysis by Category. Among single-category requests in Figure 4, MEM-SQL gains most on rephrases (R) and parametric changes (P), followed by shared joins (J). These requests preserve the historical query structure, so memory supplies the needed computation without the unrelated tables and columns that schema retrieval brings in. MEMSQL trails the baseline slightly on structural changes (S) and shared concepts (C), where memory alone is insufficient. Shared concepts need tables and columns outside memory, and structural changes may need details that MEM-SQL abstracts away to generalize its memory items. On composite categories, MEM-SQL gains clearly on P+S, P+C, S+C and J+C, since template, component, or concept can match each part of the request. It ties on S+J and trails on P+J, and these losses come from multi-source requests. On single-source requests, MEM-SQL leads the strongest baseline on both, with 68.2 and 37.9 against 67.2 and 33.3. From singleto multi-source requests, recall falls from 78% to 62% on P+J and from 89% to 65% on S+J, likely because shared-join edits rewrite filters and measures so the request no longer resembles its template or component. Memory retrieval is therefore limited when query must combine several historical sources. Appendix C.1 gives category-level results. 2 Routing Strategy by Category. MEM-SQL answers request from memory unless coverage gate finds no item above its threshold or the generator judges the gated evidence insufficient. Either case escalates the request to schema linking. Table 4 reports the share, recall and EX of each route by category. Escalations target incomplete evidence. MEM-SQL escalates 4.3% of requests, 1.1% through the coverage gate, almost all of them shared concepts, and 3.2% through the generator. sections.title: 5.5 Error Analysis
sections.content: Memory reduces table errors but not aggregation errors. Figure 5 classifies incorrect MEMSQL memory-route answers by the first applicable error found through comparison with the reference SQL. Compared with the strongest baseline AMEM, table errors fall from 31.4% to 21.4% of wrong answers, and from 55.0% to 33.7% on BEAVER. Aggregation remains the largest class for both systems, at 36.1% and 38.2%, but both have the same cause 63.6% of the time on common failures. These errors stem from question semantics that neither history nor schema linking resolves. Structural changes are most affected, with 45.2% of their errors in aggregation. Without schema, MEM-SQL also produces more invalid SQL, with execution failures at 10.8% against 3.2% for A-MEM. Appendix C.2 gives the full breakdown. sections.title: 6 Transferability of On-demand Schema Linking
sections.content: We compare OSL and USL on each memory baseline while holding the memory store and retrieval procedure fixed. Both policies use the same schema linking procedure (Wang et al., 2025b).Table 7 reports absolute values, and Figure 6 shows the changes. Figure 6: Changes when switching each retriever from USL to OSL. EX gains are percentage points and cost savings are percentages. OSL transfers its efficiency to every memory design, but its accuracy gain depends on whether retrieval returns complete evidence. Averaged over backbones, OSL cuts input tokens by at least 60% and latency by at least 34% for every memory design. For DAIL-SQL and A-MEM, accuracy rises by 6.0 and 5.1 points on requests with full recall, but not on the rest. Without coverage gate, both baselines answer most incompletely covered requests on memory, where DAIL-SQL loses 4.7 points and A-MEM gains nothing. Gains of OSL concentrate on rephrases and parametric changes, by 5.2 points for BIRD-History, 12.9 points for DAIL-SQL and 12.8 points for A-MEM. On composite requests, OSL raises A-MEMs EX by 3.1 points but lowers DAIL-SQLs by 0.6 points, consistent with DAIL-SQL retrieving full memory for only 47.6% of composite requests against 71.3% for A-MEM. BIRD-History loses accuracy on five of six backbones, with the largest drops on composite requests of 7.6 points even on the subset with full recall. Fragment-level memory alone therefore is insufficient with with-held schema.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark), benchmark that records both wholequery adaptation and partial computation reuse from past Text-to-SQL queries, with six single and six composite categories drawn from four benchmarks. We also presented MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), which stores hierarchical memory derived from verified SQL, retrieves from it through coverage gate, and consults the schema on demand through OSL. Across six language models, MEM-SQL raises mean execution accuracy while reducing generation cost. Ablations show that memory granularity matters: templates guide adaptation, while components support composition. OSL reliably cuts cost across memory designs, but its accuracy benefit depends on the design. Several limitations remain. HARE does not model schema drift, which is common in enterprise databases. concepts definition can change, for example, the month fiscal year starts. Future work could add such changes to test whether memory systems adapt. MEM-SQL is also evaluated with static memory, so how adding, updating and retiring memory affects performance in dynamic settings remains open. Finally, execution accuracy rejects answers that differ only in format, such as rounding, and cannot detect SQL that returns the right rows for the wrong reason, so future evaluation should also assess intent.

The BR1BR7 examples illustrate primitive tasks. In the primitive structural-changes category, BR12, BR13 and BR16 all preserve the CTEs WHERE, grouping grain and aggregates. Paired refers to the combinations in Table 9. Their prompts name targets in table order: parametric changes for templates, structural variation for CTE clauses, shared join path for CTE joins, and shared concepts for schema concepts. For BR14, pairs with schema concepts use structure (template: value). BR0: Rephrase Rephrase through word choice, voice, clause order, request form or schema terminology. Go beyond single synonym. Preserve scope, filters, values, grain, output, order and ties so the source SQL still answers the question. Example. Top 3 regions by shipped orders in 2023 Which three regions had the most orders shipped during 2023? BR1: Date-Window Shift Shift both bounds of date, year, month or period filter to another window of the same kind. Primitive parametric tasks preserve boundary inclusivity. Example. '2023-01-01'..'2023-12-31' '2021-01-01'..'2021-12-31'. BR2: Segment Slice Select another valid value of the same categorical filter column. Primitive parametric tasks also allow pattern filter on that column. Example. status = 'shipped' status = 'cancelled'. BR3: Threshold Move Change the cut-off of numeric comparison. In primitive parametric task, the comparison may flip only for at least at most. Example. amount > 100 amount > 2500. BR4: Top-N Resize Change of LIMIT, an OFFSET or rank cut-off. Primitive parametric tasks resize an existing cut-off. Example. LIMIT 3 LIMIT 5. BR5: Best/Worst Flip Reverse sort direction (most fewest, earliest latest). Example. DESC ASC. BR6: Entity Drill Replace an entity ID, name or code with another real value from the same column. Example. customer_id = 17 42. BR7: In-List Change Add, remove or replace IN list members using real values. Primitive parametric tasks require different list drawn from the same column. Example. IN ('web', 'store') IN ('app', 'phone', 'partner'). BR8: Granularity Change Shared joins. Change the CTEs grain on the kept joins: add or remove time or hierarchy key, or aggregate once more. Define any new bucket. Example. GROUP BY p.category GROUP BY p.category, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', o.order_date). Shared concepts. Group or bucket by time or hierarchy column the source does not use. Example. Customers with shipped order, by signup month: GROUP BY STRFTIME('%Y-%m', c.signup_date). Paired. Group or partition by finer or coarser bucket of the same dimension; define new buckets. sections.title: B Experimental Protocol
sections.content: B.1 Memory Admission MEM-SQL processes candidates in fixed order per database. Eligible neighbors must be visible, verified and from the same layer and schema version. Merge. Templates require identical SQL after case and whitespace normalization. Components must also match in version and output grain. Schema concepts require the same normalized name, column mappings and join mappings. Coverage Review. If no merge applies, the reviewer may inspect up to neighbors with cosine similarity of at least τ . Admission uses (k, τ ) = (4, 0.30) for templates, (5, 0.25) for components and (10, 0.35) for schema concepts. The reviewer checks joins, fixed predicates, slot roles and concept mappings for joint coverage. Empty neighborhoods and skipped reviews lead directly to insertion. B.2 Inference Settings Usage metadata remain fixed throughout evaluation. Each run allows 272,000 context tokens and at most three SQL-generation calls per question. At inference, per-atom (k, τ ) is (2, 0.45) for templates, (8, 0.50) for components and (2, 0.50) for schema concepts. Flat retrieval uses (25, 0.25). B.3 Baseline Adaptations DAIL-SQL. DAIL-SQL masks question tokens using schema-index terms and value heuristics, then computes normalized text-embedding-3-large vectors. It selects up to nine demonstrations, prioritizing examples
